sections.html: Butler County is in southwestern Ohio. Hamilton is both the seat and the biggest city. Population was 390,357 in 2020 and is estimated at 400,128 for July 2025. About 69.9 percent of 146,822 households are owner-occupied, with a typical home value of $258,500 and median household income of $81,590. Sixteen school districts, including Lakota, Fairfield, Hamilton, Middletown and Talawanda, reach into the county, which means your bill turns on the taxing districts your parcel sits in.

The auditor reports a median residential and agricultural increase of 19 percent for tax year 2026, payable in 2027, and a median 20 percent for commercial and industrial property. The auditor's sales ratio sits near 90 percent of full market value. Increases vary a lot by place.

Voted levies can move a bill more than value does. A new countywide 2-mill developmental disabilities levy runs about $70 per $100,000 of value, and a 4.49-mill Fairfield Township fire levy runs about $157 per $100,000. New state laws soften the effect of higher values, and second-half bills carry an inflation cap credit under House Bill 186.

Values get reset on a six-year cycle with a lighter update at the three-year mark. Locally, the last full reappraisal was 2026, the updates fell in 2023 and 2029, and 2032 is when the next full one is scheduled.

sections.h2: How the tax bill is figured
sections.html:
The math begins with fair market value as the auditor sets it. Thirty-five percent of that is your taxable value. Run it against the combined mill rate per 1,000, tack on levies and special assessments, and credits come off at the end.

  • Parcel numbers. A real estate parcel is a letter followed by 13 numbers, and about 160,000 parcels exist in the county.
  • Taxing districts. There are 66 of them, and rates differ between, say, Hamilton and Liberty Township.
  • Reduction factors. Voted levies are frozen at the dollars they first raised, so the state shaves the gross rate with a reduction factor.
  • Credits. Two credits, non-business and owner-occupancy, cover only levies that predate the November 2013 election. Homestead is its own program for qualifying seniors and disabled owners.

Special assessments for street paving or weed removal also show on the bill and go back to the government that levied them.

Bills come due in two installments. Expect mid to late February for the first and early August for the second, but trust the date printed on your bill. No bill in the mailbox? Call the treasurer at (513) 887-3181.

Because Ohio bills in arrears, a payment made in 2026 covers tax year 2025. Section 323.121 sets the late charge: 5 percent when full payment lands within the first ten days after the due date, and 10 percent after that.

Interest also builds up. On older balances it begins the first day of the month after the second-half deadline, and everything still unpaid takes another charge on December 1. You may ask for relief with an Application for Remission of Penalty, though the law grants it in few situations.

Take a value complaint to the Board of Revision. Three people sit on it: the auditor, the treasurer and one county commissioner. It looks at value only, never at how much tax you owe. Filing runs January 1 through March 31, and you can usually file just once per three-year valuation period.

  • Fill out DTE Form 1, Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, and attach your evidence of value.
  • Submit it through the office's online vendor, by email to bor@bcohio.gov, or by mail.
  • A Notice of Hearing arrives by email or certified mail.
  • Allow three to four weeks after the hearing for the Notice of Result.

Ask for a cut of $50,000 or more and a school board or another eligible party may file a counter-complaint. If you lose, you get 30 days from the mailing date to go on to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas, and the board of revision must be told too.

sections.h2: What sellers pay at the auditor and recorder
sections.html:
Every deed stops at the auditor before it reaches the recorder. There the conveyance fee is $3.00 for each thousand of sale price (round the price up to the next hundred) plus $.50 per parcel, with a $3.00 minimum on real estate. The auditor takes cash, or a check payable to the Butler County Auditor.

DTE Form 100 goes with an ordinary sale and Form 100EX with an exempt transfer. The legal description must be attached, and the Engineer's Office (513-867-5744) should approve it ahead of submission. You can send the transfer by mail, drop it off, or e-file.

The recorder's fee sheet, effective January 1, 2025, lists these charges:

  • $39.00 for a deed, mortgage or lease up to two pages, including a $5.00 preservation surcharge, and $8.00 per added page.
  • $20.00 more for a document that misses the standard layout rules.
  • $4.00 per reference for a satisfaction or release.
  • $2.00 per page for copies and $1.00 per document to certify.

Each deed needs its parcel number, a self-addressed stamped return envelope, and a prepared-by statement if the notary is in Ohio. The office quotes 24 hours for turnaround. Find it at 130 High Street in Hamilton, or call (513) 887-3192.

If a bill is still open when you sell, the balance gets settled at closing. Have the title company request a payoff figure from the treasurer, and expect unpaid tax, penalty and interest to come out of your proceeds. A cash buyer follows the same payoff routine but can close quickly, with no lender appraisal or underwriting to wait on. Before the deed heads to the auditor, make sure whoever runs the closing has confirmed the second-half amount.

Gather the parcel number, the legal description and your latest tax bill before the closing appointment. If the new value from the 2026 reappraisal looks wrong and you are still inside the window, a Board of Revision complaint can be filed before you sell, though the filing period is limited to one per three-year cycle.

faqs.q: When is the second-half Butler County tax bill due?
faqs.a: Early August is typical for the second half, with the first half landing in mid to late February. Your printed bill shows the exact day.

faqs.q: How did Butler County values change in 2026?
faqs.a: Residential and agricultural values rose by a median of 19 percent, and commercial and industrial by 20 percent. Changes differ by place, from a median 39 percent in Lemon Township to 12 percent in the city of Fairfield. New voted levies affect the bill as much as value does.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Butler County valuation every year?
faqs.a: Usually not. State law lets an owner file once per three-year valuation period, with a few listed exceptions. Use DTE Form 1 between January 1 and March 31.

faqs.q: What conveyance fee applies to a Butler County sale?
faqs.a: $3.00 for every thousand of price, rounded up to the next hundred, plus $.50 per parcel. Make the check out to the Butler County Auditor. For exempt transfers that need Form 100EX, call 513-887-3154.

faqs.q: What will the Butler County Recorder charge for a deed?
faqs.a: Two pages or fewer costs $39.00, and that already folds in the $5.00 preservation surcharge. Pages beyond that are $8.00 each, and a document with a layout problem picks up $20.00. Questions go to (513) 887-3192.
